clue.text: Leaves here with very small computer?

blocks.note: a palm tree's fronds all sprout from its crown, so this is the place at the head of the trunk
a handheld machine that sits in the hand

explanation.surface: Someone taking their leave while clutching a tiny computer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like a verb, someone departing; it is the foliage of a palm, which grows only at the top of the trunk.
explanation.definitionFit: A palmtop is a handheld computer small enough to hold in one hand, an older name for a pocket-sized device.

clue.text: European election broadcast

indicators.note: a broadcast is something put out over the air to be heard, so we go by sound

blocks.note: a poll is a vote

explanation.surface: A party political broadcast ahead of a European election.
explanation.walkthrough: 'European election' reads as one phrase, like the Euro elections; split it, and 'European' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A Pole is a native of Poland, one example of a person from Europe.

clue.text: Old world meeting for races covering about three miles?

blocks.note: an old unit of distance, roughly three miles
races spread over that distance make up a stretch of them; the question mark flags this loose sense
races as peoples, not contests

explanation.surface: A sports meeting where the runners cover a three-mile course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Races' and 'meeting' suggest athletics; races are peoples, and a league's worth of them is a League of Nations.
explanation.definitionFit: The League of Nations was the international body set up after the First World War, a forerunner of the United Nations.

clue.text: Bear with canine appearance?

blocks.note: the surface reading: an animal that looks like a dog
the setter's reading: pointed canine molars and incisors coming through, which a baby must bear

explanation.surface: A bear that looks rather like a dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear' is a verb, to endure, and 'canine' means a pointed tooth; its 'appearance' is it coming through the gum.
explanation.definitionFit: To teethe is what an infant does as its first set of milk teeth cut through, which is uncomfortable and has to be endured.

clue.text: Awkward situation, but parking's easy

blocks.note: P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking
light work is easy work

explanation.surface: A driver in a tricky spot who at least finds parking simple.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's in 'parking's' joins the two pieces, as in 'parking is (next to) easy'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plight is a dangerous, difficult or unfortunate state of affairs, a close synonym for a predicament.

clue.text: Deplored crude modern setting for university

indicators.note: crude means rough and unrefined, so these letters come in raw, unordered form
a setting holds a jewel, so one set of letters mounts another inside it

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters
U is the standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: Someone complaining about the ugly new architecture of a university campus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crude modern setting' reads as a sneer at concrete buildings; 'crude' scrambles MODERN and 'setting for' puts U inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To mourn something is to lament or grieve over it, and deplored means regretted it deeply.

clue.text: Postpone dance after union's withdrawn from opening

indicators.note: something withdrawn from a place is taken out of it, so a letter goes

blocks.note: the mouth is the body's opening, or the opening of a river or cave
U stands for union, as in RU for Rugby Union
a formal dance

explanation.surface: A dance put off after the trade union pulled out of the opening event.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue names the dance first, but 'after' sends it to the end of the answer; the 's is 'has', joining the parts.
explanation.definitionFit: To mothball a plan is to shelve it for later, like clothes packed away in naphthalene to keep insects off.

clue.text: Train due for overhaul had a leak

indicators.note: an overhaul takes machinery apart and puts it back together differently

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: A railway engine due in the workshop because it has sprung a leak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had a leak' looks like a mechanical fault on the train; it is slang for going to the toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: To take a leak is informal British and American slang for passing water, so had a leak means relieved oneself.

clue.text: See 9
Strike involving Catholic all-rounder on track

indicators.note: to involve is to include within, so one word wraps round another

blocks.note: to strike words out of a text
a standard abbreviation of Catholic

explanation.surface: An industrial strike that drags in a Catholic sportsman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strike' wants to be a walkout or a blow; here it means to cross out.
explanation.definitionFit: A decathlete competes in ten track and field events, so is an all-round athlete in athletics.

clue.text: What jewel thieves do on course to aim for a perfect job

blocks.note: stones are gems, so thorough robbers flip over every gem they find
an idiom for being exhaustively thorough

explanation.surface: Burglars well set for a flawless heist.
explanation.walkthrough: Stone is slang for a gem, so the idiom can be read literally of thieves. The answer runs from 9 across into 7 down.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to try every possible avenue, searching exhaustively until a task is completely thorough.

clue.text: Native in Turkey's elected thus

blocks.note: used as it stands
TR is the international vehicle code for Turkey
a party elected is in power
Latin for thus, used to mark a quoted error

explanation.surface: A report that a local candidate has won an election in Turkey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Native in Turkey' reads as one phrase about a Turk; 'in' is only the first piece of wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Native in the sense of inborn or inherent: an intrinsic quality belongs to something's essential nature.

clue.text: Spare no expense — but path to house needs repair

indicators.note: something needing repair is broken and has to be put back together

blocks.note: anagram fodder, fourteen letters

explanation.surface: A homeowner splashing out, though the garden path is crumbling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'But' looks like a connecting word between two halves; it is part of the fodder, supplying the B, U and T that the path lacks.
explanation.definitionFit: A British idiom: to push the boat out is to celebrate lavishly, spending generously on an occasion.

clue.text: Prominent part of male anatomy's very soft in water

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, enclosed

blocks.note: Adam's ale is a jokey old name for water, the only drink in Eden
pianissimo, the musical marking for very soft

explanation.surface: A slightly risque remark about a man's body going limp in cold water.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface steers towards a smutty reading; the anatomy is the throat, and the 's joins definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The Adam's apple is the lump of thyroid cartilage visible at the front of the throat, usually larger in men.

clue.text: Disaster when humour backfires

indicators.note: a backfire sends things in the opposite direction, so letters run back

blocks.note: humour in its old sense, a temper or state of mind

explanation.surface: A joke that falls flat and ends in catastrophe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Humour' wants to be comedy; it is a mood, as in 'in good humour'.
explanation.definitionFit: Doom is ruin or a terrible fate, and in loose usage a disaster that brings destruction.

clue.text: Obscene phone call's a bloomer

blocks.note: blue jokes and films are indecent ones
to give someone a bell is British slang for phoning them

explanation.surface: An obscene phone call dismissed as a blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: A bloomer is British for a mistake, which fits the surface; here it means a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossword-only sense: a bloomer is anything that blooms, and the bluebell is a woodland spring flower.

clue.text: Frenchman joining crew? Rot!

blocks.note: a crew or gang of workers
René, a typical French first name

explanation.surface: A scornful dismissal of a Frenchman signing up with the crew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joining' puts the two pieces side by side; the Frenchman comes second even though he is named first.
explanation.definitionFit: Gangrene is the death and decay of body tissue, a literal medical kind of rotting flesh.

clue.text: Ring an upper-class young lady up for financial assistance

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom to the top

blocks.note: to ring a number is to dial it
the indefinite article
gel is the posh pronunciation of girl

explanation.surface: Phoning a well-bred girl to ask her for money.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole of DIAL A GEL is read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Legal aid is public money paying for lawyers for those who cannot afford them, so a form of state funding.

clue.text: Orders staff appointments

blocks.note: to man something is to staff it
dates are fixed engagements

explanation.surface: A manager issuing orders about staff rotas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' looks like a noun, the employees; it is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: A mandate is an official command or instruction, so mandates are authoritative directives as a noun, or commands as a verb.

clue.text: Bird showing speed

blocks.note: a small wading shorebird
a nautical unit of velocity

explanation.surface: A bird putting on a turn of pace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Showing' only joins the two meanings; the bird is a wader, and the speed is the sailor's measure.
explanation.definitionFit: The knot is a sandpiper, and a knot is also one nautical mile per hour, used for ships and aircraft.

clue.text: Grant supporting tea house in the Alps

indicators.note: in a down entry a support holds from beneath, so the word before it goes lower, sent second

blocks.note: cha or char is British slang for tea
to let is to allow or grant

explanation.surface: A grant paying for a tea house in a Swiss resort.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, 'supporting' puts one piece below another, so LET goes under CHA.
explanation.definitionFit: A chalet is the wooden mountain cottage typical of Switzerland, with overhanging eaves.

clue.text: High-level bid around middle of slow obstacle race

indicators.note: the middle is the centre, so only the central letters are kept
to go around something is to encircle it on every side

blocks.note: in bridge a slam is a bid to win all or all but one of the tricks
the two central letters of the four

explanation.surface: An ambitious attempt at an obstacle course, with a slow patch in the middle.
explanation.walkthrough: A bridge slam is the highest level of contract, which is why the clue calls it a high-level bid.
explanation.definitionFit: A slalom is a skiing or canoeing race weaving between poles or gates, so a course full of obstacles.

clue.text: Book of star signs?

blocks.note: the surface reading: a horoscope guide to the zodiac
the setter's reading: famous people sign their names in a collector's book

explanation.surface: An astrology book listing the twelve zodiac signs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star signs' is a fixed phrase for zodiac signs; read it as celebrities signing.
explanation.definitionFit: Collectors carry a blank book in which famous people write their names, gathering celebrity signatures.

clue.text: Girl band's drink reduced in volume?

indicators.note: reduced means made smaller, so one letter is lost from what follows

blocks.note: bevvy is British slang for an alcoholic drink
V is the standard abbreviation for volume

explanation.surface: A girl group's drink going flat, or a pop act's music turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Girl band' wants to be a pop group; it means a group of girls.
explanation.definitionFit: A bevy is a collective noun for a group, traditionally of girls or women, and also of larks or quails.

clue.text: Lone chap unexpectedly on line in attempt to communicate

indicators.note: something happening unexpectedly departs from its expected order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
L is the standard abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A lonely man suddenly getting in touch on the telephone line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' puts L after the fodder, and the anagram covers all nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ringing someone is a means of trying to reach and talk to them, so it is an effort to get in touch.

clue.text: Grab end of toboggan in winter sports event

indicators.note: the end is the final part, so only the last letter is taken
being in something means sitting inside it, enclosed

blocks.note: a luge is a small sled raced feet first
its final letter

explanation.surface: Grabbing the back of a sledge during a winter race.
explanation.walkthrough: The toboggan and the luge share a scene, which disguises that one only supplies a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A lunge is a sudden forward thrust, as when snatching at something, so a grab in noun form.

clue.text: Deprived City area regularly delays nurse

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

blocks.note: second, fourth and sixth letters
to nurse is to tend or look after

explanation.surface: A poor inner-city district where the nurses are always late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'City area regularly' tempts a solver to take alternate letters of 'City area'; they give nothing useful, and 'regularly' works on 'delays'.
explanation.definitionFit: The East End is the traditionally working-class part of London east of the City, historically poor and overcrowded.

clue.text: Vainly crossing motorway after time, wanting spirit

indicators.note: to cross something is to straddle it, one piece spanning another

blocks.note: T is the standard abbreviation for time
to no purpose, as in idle threats
M1 is Britain's main north-south motorway, with the 1 read as I

explanation.surface: A pointless drive over the motorway in search of alcohol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' looks like a drink, fitting the surface; it means courage.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something timidly means doing it without courage or boldness, lacking nerve; the adverb matches the adverbial phrase.
